overview: Embalmers prepare bodies for viewing and burial. They clean and preserve the body, restore a natural appearance with cosmetics, and follow strict health and sanitation laws. O*NET rates knowledge of customer service at 4.68 out of 5 for this job and chemistry at 3.62. Most embalmers complete an associate degree in mortuary science, 86% in O*NET data, then an apprenticeship and a state license. The BLS May 2025 median is $58,780, but it is a small field, with just 3,890 jobs. Expect tight deadlines, hours that change and exposure to hazardous chemicals.
pay: Embalmers earn a median of $58,780, and the top 10% earn $77,570 or more. Ohio has the highest state median at $71,550, 22% above the national figure, followed by Pennsylvania and North Carolina. Texas has the most embalmers, 680. Many also work as funeral directors, which can raise pay.

faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $58,780 a year. The middle half earn between $48,010 and $66,130. Ohio ($71,550), Pennsylvania ($69,950) and North Carolina ($68,550) pay the most, while Iowa has the lowest state median at $39,490. Licensed funeral directors who also embalm often earn more.

faq.q: How do you become an embalmer?
faq.a: Most embalmers earn an associate degree in mortuary science, which 86% hold in O*NET data, while 14% have a bachelor's degree. After school comes an apprenticeship of about 1 to 3 years and a state license exam. There are 2 closely related majors.

O*NET rates speaking at 3.88 out of 5 for this job and active listening at 3.75, because embalmers often speak with grieving families. Self-control and attention to detail stand out as work styles. Knowledge of chemistry (3.62) matters for handling preservation fluids safely.

faq.q: What jobs are similar to embalmer?
faq.a: The closest moves are licensed practical nurses (83% match), Surgical Assistants (78%) and Coroners (75%), based on O*NET 31.0. Respiratory Therapists are a 75% match and earn $82,280, 40% more, according to BLS May 2025 data, after an associate degree program.
